extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, philosophers of mathematics, and researchers designing metrics or evaluations of mathematical proofs (including AI evaluators)
extracted.subtask_description: Empirically grounded framework for rating mathematical proofs along multiple orthogonal dimensions (aesthetics, intricacy, utility, precision). Intended to guide human and automated appraisal of proofs without collapsing distinct qualities into a single score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty, elegance, profundity; the dimension capturing perceived insight and artistic merit of a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjectives loading on this factor include: beautiful, elegant, profound, inspired. Aesthetic judgments correlate positively with perceived utility (a 'useful' proof is likelier to be called beautiful). They are also subject to social conformity (judges' aesthetic ratings shift when they know others' ratings). Examples: a proof may be called 'elegant' (high aesthetics) whether or not it is simple; aesthetic perception is modulated by expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intricacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Complexity and difficulty of execution; captures virtuosity, sophisticated or elaborate methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjectives: intricate, complicated, dense, sophisticated. Intricacy is empirically separable from aesthetics: a proof can be both intricate and beautiful (an 'inspired tour-de-force') or intricate and not beautiful. Use this axis to record how technically involved or delicate the argument is, distinct from its perceived beauty or rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Usefulness and generative power of a proof: how applicable, informative, or fruitful the argument is for further work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjectives: useful, applicable, fruitful, informative. Utility tends to be positively correlated with aesthetic judgments. Rate utility separately because a highly useful 'workhorse' proof may lack perceived beauty, and vice versa. Consider both immediate applicability and longer-term generative potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigor, careful execution, and correctness; the technical soundness and meticulousness of the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjectives: precise, rigorous, meticulous, careful. Treat precision as distinct from insight or virtuosity: a proof may be high in precision (a careful technical lemma) while low in aesthetics or utility. Use this axis to capture formal correctness and attention to detail, not conceptual novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-axis (four-dimension) evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete appraisal records separate ratings on all four roughly orthogonal axes (aesthetics, intricacy, utility, precision) rather than collapsing them into a single 'good proof' score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study's central methodological implication: collapsing these dimensions loses information. Examples of distinct profiles: high aesthetics/low intricacy (Hardy-style elegant proof), high aesthetics/high intricacy (Wiles-style tour-de-force), low aesthetics/high utility (workhorse proof), high precision/low aesthetics (technical lemma). For human or automated evaluation workflows, present separate scores or multi-dimensional profiles rather than a single aggregate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inglis–Aberdein 16-adjective instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: A short validated rating instrument consisting of 16 adjectives (four adjectives per dimension) developed via factor analysis to operationalize the four appraisal dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a practical, reliable rubric for empirical proof evaluation: four adjectives map to each of the four dimensions with high internal reliability. Use the instrument for standardized data collection or as the basis for multi-axis scoring in studies or evaluation systems. (The paper supplies the adjective set and psychometric validation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate beauty with simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical finding and normative guidance: beauty and simplicity are almost entirely unrelated; simple proofs need not be judged beautiful and intricate proofs can be judged beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject the classical doctrine that beauty equals simplicity when designing evaluative criteria or automated metrics. Avoid heuristics or features that conflate low complexity with aesthetic merit; instead, measure complexity (intricacy) and aesthetics separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish precision (rigor) from insight (aesthetics) and virtuosity (intricacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation to track rigor, insight, and technical virtuosity as separate qualities rather than treating them as a single 'quality' attribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For evaluators and AI systems, implement separate checks/metrics for formal correctness (precision), explanatory/insightful character (aesthetics), and technical sophistication (intricacy). This prevents high scores on one axis from masking deficiencies on another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for social conformity effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic judgments are influenced by knowledge of others' opinions; social conformity can shift individuals' ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When collecting or interpreting aesthetic evaluations, control for or record exposure to others' judgments (e.g., blind independent ratings vs. open review). Use methods robust to conformity effects when attempting to measure 'pure' aesthetic responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider expertise-dependent differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Expertise reshapes aesthetic perception: novice and expert ratings differ on equation/proof aesthetics; expertise matters for appraisal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate or stratify evaluations by rater expertise. When aggregating ratings, report or model how expert vs. novice assessments diverge; consider training or calibration if using non-expert raters for aesthetic judgments.
